title: Supervision 1 essay
description: Discuss the cardiovascular adjustments that occur in whole body exercise.
instructions:
This is the work to hand in for Supervision 1. Write it here, the same way you’ll write your essays in the online exam.

  • Planning. Plan your essay before you start writing, on paper if you like.
  • Equations. Type simple ones into your text, as you’d write them by hand (× is among the special characters, under Ω). For one with a fraction, use the formula tool, Σ. Say what each equation means, and then use it.
  • Diagrams. You can add diagrams, just as you can in the exam. Draw one with Insert drawing (the pencil), or use Insert picture to add a picture, such as a photo of a diagram you drew on paper. Type a caption under it. Your pictures go into the Word document with your work.
  • Pasting. As in the exam, you can copy and paste within your work, but you can’t paste in text copied from anywhere else. Write everything in your own words.
  • Saving. Your work is saved in this browser as you type, so you can stop and come back to it. It stays here until you submit it.
  • When you’ve finished, go to the submission page (the ✓ tile at the bottom right), check your work and submit it. Then hand it in as described below.

questions.title: The circulation in exercise
questions.text:
Discuss the cardiovascular adjustments that occur in whole body exercise.

Write in continuous prose, with an introduction, paragraphs that each make one point, and a conclusion. Support your argument with mechanisms, evidence and numbers from the lectures.
questions.guidance:
Read this after you’ve written your essay, and use it before the supervision to look back over what you wrote. It isn’t a model essay. It sets out the ground a good answer covers, and how the parts connect.

What the title asks. “Discuss” asks for an argument. The strongest essays organise the response around one problem: the working muscles dilate their own arterioles to get the flow they need, and the rest of the circulation must then stop the arterial pressure from falling. Every adjustment can be explained as part of that.

  • The frame. ABP = CO × TPR, CO = HR × SV, and CO = VR = (MSFP − RAP) / RvR. Define each term the first time, and come back to the equations as you go.
  • Functional hyperaemia. Flow to working muscle rises from 2–3 to about 35 mL min−1 per 100 g, about 17-fold, so the muscle’s resistance falls to about a seventeenth (and, by Poiseuille, its arterioles need only about double their radius). Muscle is about 40% of body mass, so in whole-body exercise TPR can fall to about 20% of its resting value.
  • Its two phases. The fast phase (within 2 to 20 s) is due to K+, which rises to about 10 mM within seconds and hyperpolarises the arteriolar muscle through KIR channels and the Na+/K+-ATPase (barium or ouabain cut the dilatation by about 60%), and to the muscle pump, which lowers venous pressure in the muscle. The maintained phase has overlapping causes: K+, adenosine (A2A receptors, cAMP, PKA and KATP channels), ATP and nitric oxide released from red cells as they unload O2, nitric oxide from the endothelium, and β2-adrenoceptor dilatation by circulating adrenaline. Their redundancy is why blocking one changes little. A direct effect of low PO2 on arterioles is unlikely, because PO2 doesn’t fall near them.
  • At the capillaries. More capillaries are perfused, which increases the area for exchange and shortens the distance for diffusion (Fick), so O2 extraction rises as well as flow. A rise in capillary pressure filters more fluid, so the muscle swells a little and lymph flow rises. The Bohr shift helps unloading.
  • The cardiac output. It rises about five-fold, with the heart rate about three-fold and the stroke volume by about half. The heart alone can’t do this: it can only lower RAP, and venous return can’t rise much once RAP is near zero. Venous return rises because sympathetic venoconstriction raises MSFP (perhaps three-fold) and the muscle pump about halves RvR, so VR can rise about six-fold with RAP near zero. Less vagal and more sympathetic activity raise the rate and contractility, so the heart pumps the larger return. Guyton’s curves show both curves moving up.
  • The control. Central command drives the changes: the heart rate rises even when curare stops the muscles contracting, follows perceived effort, and rises in anticipation. Feedback from muscle and joint receptors adds to it. The baroreflex is reset to a higher set point and stabilises the pressure around it, so mean ABP rises slightly (systolic more). The baroreflex can’t be the driver, or the pressure would have to fall first.
  • Redistribution. Sympathetic vasoconstriction lowers flow to the gut, the kidneys and inactive muscle, holding TPR up and diverting blood. Coronary flow rises with the heart’s work (metabolic control), cerebral flow is held roughly constant, and skin flow first falls and then rises as heat must be lost, which competes with the muscles for cardiac output.
  • The limit, for a strong conclusion. Breathing a high O2 barely improves performance, so O2 uptake in the lungs isn’t limiting in healthy people. Two legs produce less than twice the power of one, so in fit people the muscles aren’t limiting. The circulation is: the cardiac output can’t keep up with all the muscle that could dilate, so sympathetic vasoconstriction even limits flow to the working muscles, and the pressure never falls. In unfit people the muscles may limit; in heart failure the low maximal cardiac output limits, and fatigue is a key symptom.

What makes an essay stand out. Explaining, not listing: each adjustment tied to the problem it solves. Numbers, used to argue (TPR to a fifth needs CO about five times). Evidence for the mechanisms (curare, one leg against two, blockers of K+ channels and the pump), with a sense of what isn’t known. And a conclusion that answers the question.
